reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: The 'Greek warrior helmet' facial appearance, formed by a broad, high nasal bridge continuing to the forehead with hypertelorism and a short philtrum, is characteristic
Caused by deletion of the distal short arm of chromosome 4, involving the WHS critical regions
Marked prenatal and postnatal growth restriction, microcephaly and profound feeding difficulty are near-universal
Seizures, often beginning in infancy and sometimes provoked by fever, are a core feature and a major cause of morbidity
Intellectual disability is usually severe, with hypotonia and limited speech
Most deletions are de novo, but roughly a tenth arise from an unbalanced parental translocation, mandating parental karyotyping
Midline defects such as cleft lip/palate, coloboma, cardiac septal defects and genitourinary anomalies are frequent
reference.pathophysiology: Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome results from haploinsufficiency of contiguous genes within the distal 4p16.3 region, notably the WHS critical regions containing candidate genes such as WHSC1/NSD2 and LETM1. Reduced dosage of these genes, which influence chromatin regulation, calcium/ion homeostasis and neuronal function, disrupts craniofacial, cardiac and central nervous system development. Loss of LETM1 in particular is implicated in the prominent seizure phenotype. Larger deletions generally produce a more severe clinical picture, and unbalanced familial translocations can also cause the condition.
additionalDifferentials: Non-specific syndromic intellectual disability with epilepsy
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal microarray to confirm and size the 4p deletion
Karyotype and parental karyotypes to identify a familial translocation
Electroencephalography and neuroimaging to characterise the seizure disorder
Renal tract ultrasound for structural anomalies
Feeding, swallowing and nutritional assessment given severe failure to thrive
redFlags: Prolonged or clustered seizures and status epilepticus requiring urgent management
Failure to thrive and dehydration from severe feeding difficulty
Undiagnosed congenital heart disease causing cardiorespiratory compromise
reference.prognosis: Survival is variable; many infants with larger deletions have high early mortality from malformations and infection, while those surviving infancy live into adulthood with severe intellectual disability. Seizure control and nutritional support strongly influence outcome.
pitfalls: Relying on a normal karyotype when microarray is needed to detect small deletions
Neglecting parental karyotyping and misjudging recurrence risk with a translocation
Under-treating a seizure disorder that is central to morbidity
Attributing poor growth to behaviour rather than oromotor dysfunction, delaying tube feeding
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: No treatment corrects the 4p16.3 deletion, so care targets the seizures, feeding failure and developmental needs
Antiepileptic drug therapy for the core seizure disorder, which often begins in infancy and may be fever-provoked, with a rescue plan for prolonged seizures and status epilepticus
Nutritional support for the profound feeding difficulty and failure to thrive, including thickened feeds and gastrostomy where needed
Developmental support with physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy for the hypotonia, severe intellectual disability and limited speech
Surveillance and management of congenital heart disease and renal tract anomalies
Multidisciplinary follow-up across neurology, cardiology, dietetics and developmental paediatrics
Parental karyotyping and genetic counselling, as roughly a tenth of cases arise from an unbalanced parental translocation
